cases.summary: A consent choice that is genuinely balanced and worded unlike any banner: two radio buttons, no accept/reject vocabulary at all, and neither choice gated behind the other.
An account page where cancelling exists and is called End your plan. The path is present and one click away; only the word is different.
A real enrolment deadline with the reason it exists and the next intake named. A date that closes something is not a countdown.
A per-store stock table with a genuine count of 2, and a sentence saying the count is not a limit. Scarcity-adjacent because it names a small number; not scarcity, because nothing is urged.
A checkout that discloses VAT and handling in prose rather than a line-item table, leading with the amount that leaves the account. Every fee is named; none of it is shaped like a receipt.
The Japanese counterpart: two ordinary declines opening with いいえ and ending in a soft refusal, neither of them declining the benefit itself.

Three ordinary Japanese declines opening with 結構です, none of them declining the benefit itself. Guards the reject dictionary against losing 結構です: without it, a form offering three ways to decline reads as offering none.
Three ordinary declines in the shape `No, I ...`. None of them says the user does not want the benefit, which is what separates a decline from confirmshaming.
A plan comparison whose declines keep the current plan. Guards the subscribeCta patterns against matching a bare 登録 inside a decline label: 結構です、今は登録したくありません is a refusal, not a call to action.
An account page describing an active subscription, with payment and support links but no way to cancel.

The Japanese counterpart of the account page with no cancellation path, where the words a cancel link would use are present but belong to other controls. Guards the cancelLink patterns against bridging unrelated text — 「ご利用中のプラン」 and 「パスワードを変更」 sit sixty characters apart, and a wildcard wide enough to join them would report a cancel path that does not exist.
An account page with a direct cancellation link.
A checkout disclosing tax, shipping, and the total beside the item price.
A cookie banner with accept, reject, and manage preferences, and no pre-checked box.
The same balanced cookie banner, in Japanese.

A content-marketing download page: one 「資料を受け取る」 button and nothing to consent to. Guards the Japanese accept group against matching 受け取る with no object, which reads any receive button on a page mentioning ニュースレター as a consent accept with no reject beside it.
A free-trial CTA with the renewal date, the price after it, and cancellation terms beside it.
Terms and marketing consent are separate, unchecked controls.
An ordinary about page with nothing transactional on it.
The same ordinary page, in Japanese.
The same upsell dialog, with a labelled close control.
A modal whose close control is an icon button carrying only aria-label="Close this dialog".
A Japanese modal dismissed with 「あとで」. Guards the Japanese close vocabulary against covering less than the English one, which counts a soft postponement as a way out.
Neutral declines that open the way a guilt-tripping one does — a bare "No thanks", and three that continue into an ordinary reason. None of them says the user does not want the good thing.

Terms and marketing as two independent checkboxes — the shape the bundled-consent rule recommends. A rule with no near-miss negative had never been checked for staying quiet on the pattern it asks for.
Factual stock and dispatch information, with no pressure wording.
A subscribe CTA with cancellation terms in the same block.

Terms and the privacy policy in one checkbox, with marketing separate — the shape this rule recommends. Guards the bundling count against treating an agreement and its privacy policy as two topics, which is the distinction the rule's own recommendation names.
A cookie banner offers accept and nothing else — no reject, no preferences.
The same accept-only cookie banner, in Japanese.

An accept-only banner whose second control is 「この内容で結構です」 — the assenting reading of 結構です, not a decline. Guards the reject group against silencing a banner that offers no way to refuse, which is what a bare 結構です entry would do.
One checkbox covers both the terms of service and marketing email, so neither can be refused alone.
One checkbox bundling 利用規約 with キャンペーンのお知らせ, in Japanese.
A marketing consent checkbox is checked before the user touches it; the analytics one is not.
The same pre-checked marketing consent, in Japanese.

The same pre-checked marketing box, written as checked="yes". HTML treats a boolean attribute as true whatever its value, so detection must not depend on the spelling — and the safe remediation, which removes only the spellings whose meaning is beyond argument, deliberately does not reach this one.
A checkout showing a bare item price; the only shipping wording is a footer link far from the cart.
A Japanese checkout showing a price with no 税込/送料/手数料 disclosure nearby.
The decline button shames the user for declining.

A Japanese decline worded to name what is given up: 「お得な情報はいりません」. The confirmshaming finding is the point; the page also guards the Japanese reject group against missing いりません, which would report a form offering a decline as offering none.
An upsell dialog whose only control is the upgrade button.
A Japanese newsletter modal with no 閉じる control and no dismiss affordance.
A sale page with a running countdown element.
A Japanese sale page with a running clock. 期間限定 appears in the title and the body, so the scarcity phrase rule fires too — both are true.
An unverifiable stock-pressure claim beside the buy button.
The same stock-pressure claim, in Japanese.

A real subscribe CTA that contains a negation — "Don't miss out — subscribe now" — beside a decline that also contains the verb. Guards the refusal check against reading the negation as attached to anything but the action, which would silence a genuine CTA.
The Japanese counterpart: 「見逃さないよう登録する」 negates 見逃す, not 登録, so it stays a subscribe CTA — while 「結構です、今は登録したくありません」 beside it must not be reported as one.
A subscribe CTA with a price and no cancellation terms anywhere near it.

tolerated.why: A reviewer could score this either way. The page genuinely offers no cancellation path, which is what that rule flags on a subscription-context page — and reporting the same gap twice, once for the CTA and once for the page, is arguably one problem counted twice. Neither reading is credited or penalised here.

cases.summary: A free-trial CTA with nothing nearby about what happens when the trial ends.
A Japanese free-trial CTA with no 自動更新 or 課金 disclosure nearby. 「無料トライアルを始める」 is also a subscribe CTA with no cancellation terms, which is equally true of the page.

A Japanese government design-system modal: a <dialog> whose header carries a close control labelled 閉じる, in BEM class names this project has never written. Guards the modal rule against reporting a dialog's own descendants — the close button among them — as modals of their own.

The same design system's warning banner: 偽SNSアカウントにご注意ください, a timestamp, two action buttons, and a dismiss control. Public-safety urgency wording that is not a sales tactic, in markup this project did not choose.
A Semantic-UI marketing landing page that repeats Sign Up and Get Started as links rather than buttons and never mentions a subscription, a price, or a renewal.
A Semantic-UI sign-in page whose submit control is a <div>, not a <button>, and whose only other action is a Sign Up link.
Dismissible Bootstrap-convention alerts with role="alert", the same text-less close control, and pairs of action buttons. The non-modal counterpart of the page above, and quiet.

Three Bootstrap-convention modals whose close control carries no text at all, only class="btn-close" and aria-label="Close". Guards the modal rule against requiring a textual close label, and against reporting a modal's title and body as modals of their own.
